The system is configured to sense a high-aspect-ratio nanostructure, the high-aspect-ratio nanostructure comprising at least one face having a slope with a slope angle, relative to the surface of the sample, that exceeds a predetermined threshold angle. The system comprises a metrology frame, a sample support structure for supporting a sample, and a sensor head including a probe, wherein the probe comprises a cantilever and a probe tip. The scanning probe microscopy system further comprises an actuator for scanning the probe tip relative to the substrate surface to map the nanostructures. The invention relates to a scanning probe microscopy system used to map nanostructures on the surface of a sample. The system is configured to detect a high-aspect-ratio nanostructure, which includes at least one side or face having a slope angle, measured relative to the sample surface, that is greater than a preset threshold angle.

The system includes a metrology frame, a support structure for holding the sample, and a sensor head provided with a probe. The probe includes both a cantilever and a probe tip. The scanning probe microscopy system also includes an actuator that moves the probe tip relative to the substrate surface so that the nanostructures can be mapped.

To detect the high-aspect-ratio nanostructure, the probe tip is positioned at a fixed offset angle relative to the sensor head, causing the probe tip to be inclined with respect to the sample surface. The system further includes a sensor head carrier that receives the sensor head. The sensor head carrier and the sensor head each include cooperating mounting features that together create a kinematic mount with at least three contact points, allowing the sensor head to be removably mounted on the sensor head carrier.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a scanning probe microscopy system configured for mapping nanostructures on a surface of a sample. In particular, the system is suitable for inspecting and measuring nanostructures having a high aspect ratio, including structures that include at least one face with a slope angle exceeding a predetermined threshold. Such structures can be difficult to characterize using conventional probe arrangements, especially when steep or nearly vertical sidewalls must be sensed accurately.

The system comprises a metrology frame that provides a stable mechanical reference for measurement operations. A sample support structure is arranged relative to the metrology frame and is configured to hold a substrate or sample having a surface on which the nanostructures are formed. A sensor head is provided for interacting with the sample surface. The sensor head includes a cantilever and a probe tip connected to or supported by the cantilever. During operation, the probe tip is brought into proximity with the sample surface and is used to sense the topography or other characteristics of the nanostructures.

An actuator is provided to generate relative scanning movement between the probe tip and the substrate surface. The actuator may move the probe tip, the sample support structure, or both, so that the probe tip scans across the sample surface in a controlled manner. This scanning motion enables the system to acquire measurement data representative of the shape, position, and dimensions of the nanostructures.

To improve measurement of high aspect ratio features, the probe tip is arranged at a fixed offset angle relative to the sensor head. As a result, when the sensor head is positioned relative to the sample, the probe tip is angled with respect to the sample surface rather than being oriented substantially normal to it. This angled configuration allows the probe tip to access and sense steeply inclined or sidewall surfaces of nanostructures more effectively, including faces whose slope angle exceeds the predetermined slope angle.

The sensor head is detachably mounted on a sensor head carrier. The detachable connection is implemented using a kinematic mount having at least three contact points. This mounting arrangement provides a reproducible and mechanically well-defined positioning of the sensor head relative to the carrier, while also allowing the sensor head to be removed and replaced when required. The kinematic mount thereby supports accurate alignment, repeatable measurement conditions, and convenient exchange of sensor heads, for example when different probe tip geometries or offset angles are desired for different measurement tasks.
outputs.L4:
A scanning probe microscopy system is provided for accurately mapping nanostructures having high aspect ratios, including structures with steep sidewalls, narrow trenches, deep cavities, undercut features, or other geometries that are difficult to measure using a conventional vertically oriented probe. The system includes a sensor head carrying a probe tip that is fixed at a predetermined offset angle relative to the sensor head and relative to the surface of a sample being examined. Instead of extending substantially perpendicular to the sample surface, the probe tip is inclined so that it can approach and interact with sidewall regions of a nanostructure that would otherwise be inaccessible or only partially measurable.

In operation, the angled probe tip is brought into proximity with the sample surface and scanned across a selected region. Because the probe is mounted at an offset angle, the sensing end of the tip can contact or detect steeply inclined faces of high-aspect-ratio features while reducing interference between the probe body, the sensor head, and adjacent portions of the sample. This configuration allows the system to collect topographical information from surfaces that are nearly vertical or recessed, thereby improving the completeness and accuracy of three-dimensional nanoscale measurements.

The probe may be used with known scanning probe microscopy techniques, including atomic force microscopy, scanning tunneling microscopy, or other contact, non-contact, or intermittent-contact sensing modes. The sensor head may include a cantilever, force sensor, optical detection arrangement, piezoresistive detector, capacitive detector, or another sensing mechanism suitable for detecting interaction between the probe tip and the sample. During scanning, relative motion between the probe and the sample may be controlled by one or more precision actuators, such as piezoelectric stages, flexure stages, nanopositioners, or a combination thereof.

To improve positioning accuracy and repeatability, the sensor head is preferably mounted to the instrument by means of a detachable kinematic mount. The kinematic mount includes at least three defined contact points that constrain the position and orientation of the sensor head in a reproducible manner. These contact points may be formed by cooperating balls, grooves, flats, cones, V-grooves, or other precision locating features. When the sensor head is removed and later reinstalled, the kinematic mount returns the sensor head to substantially the same position and angular orientation, thereby minimizing alignment errors and reducing the need for time-consuming recalibration.

The detachable nature of the mount also allows different sensor heads or probe-tip assemblies to be exchanged depending on the measurement task. For example, probes having different offset angles, tip lengths, stiffnesses, materials, or sensing modalities may be installed to accommodate different nanostructure geometries or sample materials. A smaller offset angle may be selected for moderately sloped features, while a larger offset angle may be selected for near-vertical sidewalls or deeply recessed structures. Because the mount provides repeatable mechanical registration, such probe changes can be performed efficiently while maintaining measurement precision.

The system may further include alignment features, locking elements, magnetic or mechanical retention devices, and electrical or optical coupling interfaces that engage when the sensor head is seated in the kinematic mount. These components help ensure stable operation during scanning while preserving the ability to remove and replace the sensor head when required. The contact points of the kinematic mount may be arranged to resist vibration, thermal drift, and mechanical play, thereby enhancing the stability of nanoscale measurements.

By combining an angled probe geometry with a repeatable detachable mounting arrangement, the scanning probe microscopy system enables reliable measurement of complex three-dimensional nanostructures that are challenging for conventional probe configurations. The angled probe improves access to steep and recessed surfaces, while the kinematic mount maintains precise sensor head positioning across repeated installations. As a result, the system provides improved capability for dimensional metrology, process monitoring, defect inspection, and characterization of advanced nanoscale devices and materials.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in how we communicate. It is called a definite article, and it helps point to something specific. For example, saying “a book” could mean any book, but saying “the book” tells us that the speaker and listener know which book is being discussed.

Although “the” is short, it adds clarity and precision to sentences. It helps organize meaning, guide attention, and make language more understandable. Without “the,” many sentences would sound incomplete or unclear. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future” show how this simple word can connect us to ideas that feel familiar and important.

In writing, “the” often goes unnoticed because it appears so frequently. However, its presence makes communication smoother and more natural. It reminds us that even the smallest words can have a powerful effect on meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate patent claim language for an invention involving scanning probe microscopy of nanostructures on a sample surface, where the probe tip is tilted relative to the sensor head and the sensor head is removably mounted on a carrier by a kinematic mount?
counterfactuals.output:
Below is example patent claim language that could be adapted for an invention involving scanning probe microscopy of nanostructures on a sample surface, with a tilted probe tip and a removably mounted sensor head using a kinematic mount.

---

## Example Claims

### 1. Independent Apparatus Claim

1. **A scanning probe microscopy apparatus** for imaging nanostructures on a surface of a sample, the apparatus comprising:  
   
   a carrier configured to be positioned relative to the sample;  
   
   a sensor head removably mounted to the carrier;  
   
   a probe supported by the sensor head and comprising a probe tip configured to interact with the surface of the sample; and  
   
   a kinematic mount coupling the sensor head to the carrier, the kinematic mount defining a repeatable mounting position of the sensor head relative to the carrier;  
   
   wherein the probe tip is oriented at a tilt angle relative to the sensor head such that, during scanning of the sample surface, the probe tip approaches the nanostructures at an oblique angle.

---

### 2. Dependent Claims

2. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount comprises at least three contact interfaces defining six degrees of constraint between the sensor head and the carrier.

3. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount comprises a plurality of spherical, conical, V-groove, or flat contact elements.

4. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount comprises a three-point mount.

5. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount is configured to allow removal and replacement of the sensor head while maintaining a predetermined spatial relationship between the sensor head and the carrier.

6. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the tilt angle of the probe tip relative to the sensor head is between about 5 degrees and about 45 degrees.

7. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the tilt angle of the probe tip relative to the sensor head is between about 10 degrees and about 30 degrees.

8. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the probe tip is tilted relative to an axis normal to the sample surface during scanning.

9. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the probe tip is tilted relative to a longitudinal axis of the sensor head.

10. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the tilted orientation of the probe tip enables imaging of sidewalls or undercut regions of the nanostructures.

11. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the probe comprises a cantilever having the probe tip disposed at a distal end thereof.

12. The apparatus of claim 11, wherein the probe tip extends from the cantilever at a non-perpendicular angle.

13. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the sensor head comprises a deflection sensor configured to detect movement of the probe.

14. The apparatus of claim 13, wherein the deflection sensor comprises an optical beam deflection sensor, an interferometric sensor, a capacitive sensor, a piezoresistive sensor, or a piezoelectric sensor.

15. The apparatus of claim 1, further comprising an actuator configured to scan the probe tip relative to the sample surface.

16. The apparatus of claim 15, wherein the actuator is configured to move at least one of the carrier, the sensor head, the probe, or the sample.

17. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount comprises a magnetic preload configured to urge the sensor head against the carrier.

18. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the kinematic mount comprises a mechanical spring preload configured to urge the sensor head against the carrier.

19. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the sensor head includes an electrical interface that is releasably coupled to a corresponding electrical interface of the carrier when the sensor head is mounted to the carrier.

20. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the sensor head includes an optical interface that is repeatably aligned with an optical path of the carrier by the kinematic mount.

21. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the carrier is mounted on a scanner stage of an atomic force microscope.

22. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the scanning probe microscopy apparatus is configured for atomic force microscopy.

23. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the probe tip is configured for contact mode, tapping mode, non-contact mode, lateral force mode, or critical dimension measurement.

24. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the nanostructures comprise semiconductor device features.

25. The apparatus of claim 1, wherein the nanostructures comprise trenches, fins, pillars, lines, vias, or gratings.

---

### 3. Independent Method Claim

26. **A method of scanning probe microscopy of nanostructures on a sample surface**, the method comprising:  
   
   mounting a sensor head to a carrier using a kinematic mount, the kinematic mount defining a repeatable position of the sensor head relative to the carrier;  
   
   positioning a probe tip supported by the sensor head adjacent to the sample surface, wherein the probe tip is tilted relative to the sensor head;  
   
   scanning the probe tip relative to the nanostructures while maintaining the probe tip at an oblique angle relative to the sample surface or relative to the sensor head; and  
   
   detecting an interaction between the probe tip and the sample surface to generate measurement data representative of the nanostructures.

---

### 4. Dependent Method Claims

27. The method of claim 26, further comprising removing the sensor head from the carrier and subsequently remounting the sensor head to the carrier using the kinematic mount.

28. The method of claim 27, wherein remounting the sensor head restores the sensor head to the repeatable position within a predetermined positional tolerance.

29. The method of claim 26, wherein scanning the probe tip comprises imaging sidewalls of the nanostructures.

30. The method of claim 26, wherein scanning the probe tip comprises measuring a critical dimension of at least one of the nanostructures.

31. The method of claim 26, wherein mounting the sensor head comprises seating a plurality of contact elements of the sensor head against corresponding contact elements of the carrier.

32. The method of claim 26, further comprising applying a magnetic or spring preload to retain the sensor head against the carrier.

33. The method of claim 26, wherein detecting the interaction comprises detecting deflection of a cantilever supporting the probe tip.

34. The method of claim 26, wherein the probe tip is tilted at an angle between about 5 degrees and about 45 degrees relative to the sensor head.

35. The method of claim 26, further comprising replacing the sensor head with a second sensor head having a second probe tip tilted at a different tilt angle.

36. The method of claim 35, further comprising selecting the second sensor head based on a geometry of the nanostructures to be imaged.

---

### 5. Additional Independent System Claim

37. **A scanning probe microscope system** comprising:  
   
   a sample support configured to hold a sample having nanostructures on a surface thereof;  
   
   a carrier movable relative to the sample support;  
   
   a removable sensor head;  
   
   a kinematic mounting assembly releasably coupling the removable sensor head to the carrier and configured to repeatably locate the removable sensor head in a predetermined position relative to the carrier;  
   
   a probe coupled to the removable sensor head, the probe having a probe tip tilted relative to the removable sensor head; and  
   
   control electronics configured to cause relative scanning movement between the probe tip and the sample surface and to receive a signal corresponding to interaction between the probe tip and the nanostructures.

---

### 6. Further Dependent System Claims

38. The system of claim 37, wherein the kinematic mounting assembly comprises three pairs of mating contact structures.

39. The system of claim 38, wherein the three pairs of mating contact structures comprise ball-and-groove, ball-and-cone, or ball-and-flat contact structures.

40. The system of claim 37, wherein the removable sensor head is one of a plurality of interchangeable sensor heads, each interchangeable sensor head having a respective probe tip tilt angle.

41. The system of claim 40, wherein the control electronics are configured to receive an identifier corresponding to the mounted sensor head and adjust a scanning parameter based on the identifier.

42. The system of claim 37, wherein the tilted probe tip is configured to reduce shadowing or improve access to vertical or reentrant surfaces of the nanostructures.

43. The system of claim 37, wherein the kinematic mounting assembly repeatably aligns at least one of an electrical connection, an optical beam path, or a mechanical reference surface between the removable sensor head and the carrier.

44. The system of claim 37, wherein the carrier comprises a magnetic element and the removable sensor head comprises a magnetically attractable element, or vice versa, to provide preload for the kinematic mounting assembly.

45. The system of claim 37, wherein the probe tip is tilted in a direction substantially parallel to a scan direction.

46. The system of claim 37, wherein the probe tip is tilted in a direction transverse to a scan direction.

47. The system of claim 37, wherein the probe tip is tilted relative to the removable sensor head by a fixed tilt angle determined by a geometry of the probe or by a mounting geometry of the probe on the removable sensor head.

48. The system of claim 37, wherein the removable sensor head comprises an adjustment mechanism configured to set or vary the tilt angle of the probe tip.

---

### 7. Alternative Broad Independent Claim

49. **An apparatus for nanoscale surface metrology**, comprising:  
   
   a carrier;  
   
   a removable sensor module kinematically mounted to the carrier; and  
   
   a scanning probe carried by the removable sensor module, the scanning probe comprising a tip tilted relative to the removable sensor module,  
   
   wherein the kinematic mounting of the removable sensor module to the carrier provides repeatable mechanical registration of the scanning probe relative to the carrier after removal and replacement of the removable sensor module.

---

### 8. Alternative Method Claim Focused on Interchangeability

50. **A method of configuring a scanning probe microscope**, comprising:  
   
   selecting, from a plurality of sensor heads, a sensor head having a probe tip tilted at a selected angle relative to the sensor head;  
   
   removably attaching the selected sensor head to a carrier using a kinematic mount;  
   
   using the kinematic mount to establish a repeatable mechanical reference between the selected sensor head and the carrier; and  
   
   scanning a sample surface containing nanostructures with the tilted probe tip.

---

These claims can be further tailored depending on whether the inventive emphasis is primarily on the tilted probe geometry, the removable kinematically mounted sensor head, the combination of both, or the use of interchangeable tilted-tip sensor heads for nanoscale metrology.
